reviewers.assessment: RQ1 directly adjudicates two rival accounts in the literature: a green wage premium (Curtis and Marinescu; Godoy and Isaksen; IMF) versus a legacy/brown premium rooted in rent-sharing and unions (Godoy and Isaksen brown premium; Colmer et al. conditional parity). Within-occupation comparison inside one industry isolates establishment wage-setting from occupational skill.

Cell-level OEWS data support employment-weighted regressions with occupation-by-year fixed effects and clustered errors by occupation. Overlapping three-year OEWS samples mean year-to-year changes are smoothed; trend claims must be cautious and descriptive. RQ2 and RQ3 can be absorbed as components of RQ1. RQ4 has a fatal identification flaw.

Energy-workforce reports (USEER 2024; Brookings 2019) emphasize the job-quality of clean energy but rarely compare like-for-like occupations across generation sources. 2021-2025 brackets the IRA prevailing wage and apprenticeship provisions, making the trend substantively timely.
Energy Policy readers care about just-transition wage implications; a short, transparent descriptive paper with clear policy relevance fits the journal's full-length article format (<= 8,000 words).

Risks: (a) no worker-level controls, so gaps may reflect unobserved worker quality or regional cost of living; (b) small cells for geothermal and biomass; (c) top-coding of high wages; (d) OEWS discourages time-series comparison. None is fatal if the paper frames estimates as descriptive establishment-side gaps, reports cell counts, uses sampling-error weights in robustness, and treats trends as smoothed.
